query: For phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys, what single intervention could improve glass-forming ability and the thermal stability of the amorphous state? Formulate one testable hypothesis that specifies the intervention without presupposing its class, the mechanism by which it would act, the predicted improvement relative to an otherwise comparable baseline, the conditions under which it should or should not work, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a minimal high‐entropy micro‐alloying additive into a phosphorus‐containing high‐entropy (or compositionally complex) alloy will enhance its glass‐forming ability and extend the thermal stability of its amorphous state.
generation.material_initial_state: A phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloy that, under standard cooling conditions, tends to crystallize or exhibits a thermally unstable amorphous phase.
generation.intervention: Incorporate a very small (e.g., 1–3 atomic %) dose of a secondary element to increase the mixing entropy without drastically changing the overall composition.
generation.conditions: This intervention is expected to work when the cooling rate or processing conditions allow the alloy to reach a regime where configurational entropy is the dominant factor influencing the liquid-to-glass transition. It may not be effective if the additive concentration is too high (risking phase separation) or under extremely rapid quenching where kinetics override thermodynamic stabilization.
generation.structural_mediator: An increased atomic-scale homogeneity and configurational diversity that effectively lowers liquid fragility and resistance to crystallization.
generation.mechanism: The high-entropy micro-alloying enhances the mixing entropy of the liquid alloy, thereby reducing its fragility. This in turn helps suppress nucleation of crystalline phases during cooling and stabilizes the amorphous structure at elevated temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a control alloy without the additive, the modified alloy should exhibit a higher glass transition temperature, a delayed onset of crystallization during heating, and measurable indicators of reduced fragility.
generation.baseline: The phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy processed under identical conditions but lacking the high-entropy micro-alloying additive.
generation.boundary: The effect is limited to low additive concentrations; values exceeding the optimal range may lead to phase inhomogeneity or unintended crystalline compound formation. Additionally, the benefits rely on processing conditions that allow thermodynamic factors to dominate.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal identity and precise concentration of the micro-alloying additive remain uncertain, and quantitative improvements in glass-forming ability and thermal stability have not been precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy samples: one set with the proposed micro-alloying additive (e.g., 2 at% of a selected element) and one set without it. Both sets should be processed under identical, controlled cooling conditions. Analyze the resulting samples for their glass-forming ability and thermal stability.
measurements: Differential scanning calorimetry to record the glass transition (Tg) and crystallization onset temperatures
X-ray diffraction analyses to assess amorphous versus crystalline phase content
Dynamic mechanical analysis or other methods to determine the liquid fragility index
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the micro-alloyed samples do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in Tg, a delayed crystallization onset, and reduced liquid fragility relative to the control samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Separating the Role of Mixing‐Entropy on the Dynamics of Glass‐Forming Liquids

Abstract: AbstractWhile the concept of high entropy has gained prominence in materials design, disentangling specific impacts of entropy on material properties from the enthalpy of mixing remains elusive. It is demonstrated that the role of entropy can be distinguished from the dynamics of glass‐forming liquids through micro‐alloying. Based on experiment analysis of 79 compositions, liquid fragility is found to consistently decreases under two conditions: i) when the alloying content x is minimal, irrespective of the elements used; or ii) when increasing the diversity of alloying elements at a constant x, namely the high‐entropy micro‐alloying. These observations are consistent with thermodynamic principles that favor an entropy‐dominated regime over enthalpy. These findings elucidate the subtle impact of mixing entropy on material properties and provide evidence of the entropy nature of glass transition. This research innovates by distinguishing entropy’s impact from enthalpy in materials through micro‐alloying. It finds liquid fragility decreases with minimal alloying content or increased element dive
